Focus was on schema enforcement, guardrails, and validation for Novus's catalog enrichment pipeline. Customer liked deterministic JSON outputs and built-in fallbacks; concerns about latency at peak QPS and VPC/private deployment options. Agreed to pilot with Dedicated capacity and run benchmarks on sample traffic.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-05
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen, Diego Morales, Priya Rao (Redwood); Maya Patel, Ethan Brooks, Luis Gomez (Novus)
Shared artifacts: deck: https://redwood-demo.company/decks/structured-output, sample binder: https://redwood.sheets/novus-prompt-set

00:00 Avery: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Avery from Redwood, AE on this account, and with me is Diego our SE. Quick intro?
00:08 Maya: Hi, Maya here, Head of ML at Novus Retail. We own the product catalog enrichment pipeline.
00:12 Luis: Luis, CTO — mostly listening, want to understand infra/security implications.
00:16 Ethan: Ethan, Platform, I'll be running the pilot infra.
00:22 Diego: Cool, we'll go through structured output demo, JSON mode, function/tool calling, and show Console + Optimize recommendations. We'll keep it practical.
00:30 Avery: Quick context — Novus wants deterministic JSON from generative steps so downstream services can parse and store results cleanly, and to add tool-calls for price lookup and inventory checks.
00:42 Maya: Yes, exactly. We need schema enforcement and guardrails — and auditability for compliance.
00:47 Diego: Great. I'll share my screen — starting with API JSON mode. Note, we'll use a simple catalog enrichment example: input product title + attributes -> outputs structured JSON with normalized brand, category, and attributes.
01:10 Diego: (demo) Here's the Redwood API call, mode: structured_output, schema attached. You can see we paste a JSON Schema that defines fields: brand:string, category:enum[clothing, electronics,...], attributes:object (key-values). Schema validation runs server side and there's a validation error payload if the model returns unexpected types.
01:35 Maya: Are those schemas editable in Console?
01:38 Diego: Yep, Console supports creating named schemas, versioning, and pinning to model endpoints. You can also associate guardrails — like reject outputs that don't match, or auto-correct with a secondary pass.
01:50 Avery: For Novus, you can enforce a strict reject policy so anything that fails schema triggers a retry or fallback to a conservative model.
01:58 Ethan: How does the function/tool calling fit? We want the model to call an internal price-check service and a taxonomy service during generation.
02:05 Diego: Two ways — inline tool calling from the API (function-calling primitives) or orchestrated via Console workflows. Example: model returns a function call {"tool":"price_lookup","args":{"sku":"123"}}; Redwood will call the registered tool (we can configure auth and vpc egress rules) and feed the result back into the model.
02:30 Maya: Ok and that tool sits in our VPC? We need it to be internal.
02:35 Diego: Yes — for Private deployments or Dedicated with VPC peering you can register a tool endpoint reachable only over the VPC. For hosted we support secure egress via private link or customer-managed NAT.
02:48 Luis: From security view: SSO, RBAC, KMS?
02:52 Avery: We support SAML SSO, fine-grained RBAC in Console, audit logs for every request, and customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM integrations. We'll share the security whitepaper after.
03:05 Maya: Can we see an end-to-end run?
03:08 Diego: Yep. Running live: sample prompt -> model produces JSON with a function call for price lookup -> Redwood calls Novus price service -> merges price back and returns final JSON.
03:25 (screen) Model output: {"brand":"Acme Co", "category":"clothing", "attributes": {"color":"navy"}, "tools": [{"tool":"price_lookup" ,"args":{"sku":"SKU-987"}}]}
03:42 Ethan: Nice. How do you prevent hallucinated tool calls or arg tampering?
03:48 Diego: We validate tool args against declared input schemas and can enforce a whitelist of allowed tools per customer. There's also a pre-exec hook where you can run a quick arg validation lambda. If validation fails, we return structured error and optionally fall back.
04:05 Maya: What about streaming and partial outputs? Our pipeline consumes incremental tokens as they arrive.
04:09 Diego: Structured mode supports streaming; each chunk includes partial JSON fragments plus a final 'validation' envelope. For consumers we provide a deterministic reassembly helper in our SDK. We also have a KV/prefix cache for repeated identical context to reduce cost.
04:25 Luis: Latency is a concern — peak QPS around 600 for enrichment, p95 latency target 250ms.
04:33 Diego: For that profile we'd recommend Dedicated pools sized with GPU instances optimized for low-latency models, plus auto-batching tuned to small batch sizes to keep token latency low. Our Optimize product will suggest batch size and quantization profile based on your prompt distribution.
04:55 Avery: We can run a baseline: Diego will run the Redwood benchmark with your sample traffic and return p50/p95 cost estimates.
05:02 Ethan: Good. Regarding cost, can we fall back to cheaper model for non-critical attributes?
05:07 Diego: Yes — routing policies support model variants by route/attribute and automatic fallback if higher-tier capacity is saturated. You can pin critical routes to low-latency variants.
05:18 Maya: Show me the Console flow for schema creation and rollout.
05:22 Diego: (Console demo) Create Schema -> attach to Model Endpoint -> set enforcement: reject|correct|warn -> set rollout: canary to 5% then 100% with automatic rollback on schema regression. We also tie regression alerts to labeled prompt sets so you get notified if sample outputs fail.
06:00 Maya: If a schema update is needed mid-run, what's the process?
06:04 Diego: We version schemas. You can deploy a new schema and do a canary run. For running jobs we offer on-the-fly compatibility checks and we won't change enforcement behavior mid-request.
06:15 Ethan: For our pilot, we want to test three flows: brand normalization, category mapping, and price/inventory tool calls.
06:22 Avery: Sounds good. We'll scope pilot to those. Diego, can you capture what infra we need?
06:27 Diego: We'll need sample traffic (Ethan), a VPC endpoint for tool calls (Novus infra), and decision on Dedicated vs Private. For Dedicated we'll provision an isolated GPU pool and test.
06:40 Maya: Anything in the demo about guardrails for PII? We have product descriptions that may include customer initials etc.
06:46 Diego: You can configure the pipeline to strip PII before sending to model (preprocessor rule), mask in logs, and redact in audit logs. We also support retention policies per customer.
06:58 Luis: How are audit logs delivered?
07:01 Avery: You can stream audit logs to your cloud bucket or SIEM; for Private deployments logs remain in your control.
07:08 Maya: Ok can we switch to a slightly tougher prompt, one with ambiguous brand text?
07:12 Diego: Sure. Running ambiguous sample... model first hypothesizes brand candidates, then triggers taxonomy tool for disambiguation, returns a ranked list with confidence and chosen canonical.
07:32 Model (transcribed): "um, it's likely 'Acme Co' or 'Acme Corporation' — calling taxonomy service for best match"
07:40 Maya: I like the confidence scores. If confidence < 0.6 we want a manual review flag.
07:44 Diego: You can configure automatic flags: if confidence threshold fail -> create a ticket in your queue or route to human-in-the-loop.
07:55 Ethan: Regarding function calling auth — how do we provide credentials for the registered tool?
07:59 Diego: We store tool credentials encrypted with your KMS and inject them at call-time only over the VPC/private link. For hosted we support short-lived tokens via your identity provider.
08:12 Maya: Any rate-limiting or quotas per tool?
08:15 Diego: Yes, per-tool and per-route rate limits; you can also set throttling rules in Console.
08:20 Luis: For pilot success criteria — we'd like <5% schema rejects, p95 latency <300ms, and accuracy target for brand normalization >92%.
08:29 Avery: We'll put that into the pilot SLA and measurement plan.
08:34 Priya (joined briefly): Quick note — Optimize will run and give suggested quantization and batching that balances p95 and cost. We saw good results for similar retailers.
08:45 Maya: Good. One question on rollback: if new model regresses on a labeled eval set, can we auto-rollback to previous model?
08:52 Diego: Yes — you can configure automatic rollback on regression triggers tied to your eval set and example prompts.
09:05 Maya: Any gotchas with streaming structured outputs and JSON validity under interrupted streams?
09:09 Diego: We include a stream envelope with sequence numbers and final validation checksum. SDK helpers will wait for final chunk and validate. If validation fails, you can re-request the finalization pass or run the correction flow.
09:25 Ethan: For our data retention and compliance we need logs only for 90 days and must route everything through our KMS.
09:30 Avery: That's supported — retention is configurable and KMS integration is standard for Dedicated/Private.
09:36 Maya: Ok, I want to check the sample error payloads.
09:40 Diego: Example: {"error":"schema_validation_failed", "details": ["attributes.color expected string but got array"]} — and we include a 'fix_suggestions' field when auto-correction is enabled.
09:58 Luis: Very helpful. On the security docs, please include details about penetration testing cadence and SOC2 report access.
10:05 Avery: Will do.
10:08 Diego: Wrapping up — recapping next steps: pricing, security docs, sample prompts, benchmark run, and schedule deep-dive next week.
10:20 Maya: Thanks — excited to try the pilot.
10:23 Luis: Thanks all.
10:25 End of meeting.

Notes on transcript quality: There are a few transcription errors, some tool names transcribed oddly, and occasional speaker attribution mistakes; the demo included live code snippets and the screen share produced some clipped audio during the tool call example.
